Well actually I don't really agree about it being good game design. Even though SMB is far better than any of the other "rage games" mentioned, the combination of extremely demanding levels plus short respawn merely means that you can brute-force through every level with very little actual thinking or even understanding of mechanics going into it.

It's like a musician learning to play a sheet perfectly, playing it once then forgetting about it forever. The levels are so rigid that in actual gameplay, SMB plays more like a rythm game than a platformer, which makes everything extremely contrived but I'll get to that later. You have to input a pre-defined sequence of controls with extremely tight windows i.e. learn each level individually with very little skill actually carrying over to the next one. Which leads me to the controls. I cannot agree on the controls being even close to what I would call "tight". They are extremely floaty. That combined with the sometimes absurd movement speed effectively reinforces the need to play each level like a music sheet rather than reacting to what happens on the screen. Actually, the floaty-ness of the controls even forces you to avoid trusting what's shown on screen because of how backwards and unintuitive they are. It devolves into a pure exercise in muscle memory in the later levels that I personally didn't enjoy all that much.

Now consider Hotline Miami, which is a game that has many similarities with SMB. Namely, very demanding levels and instant respawn. However, HM introduces random elements into levels and lets you think about your approach. In a sense, the experience of playing HM is much more interactive than that of playing SMB. Also, HM has controls that make sense and react immediately, despite the infamous screen swaying.

Disclaimer: I played the PC version of SMB with a keyboard. My bad experience with it might be down to that.

In psychology, there exists the diathesis-stress model, which is essentially biology+environment+stress=manifestation of mental disorder. It's the idea that your genetics decide to what degree you can expect a certain mental disorder, and your environment (and most importantly the stressors in it) decide when and how this disorder forms. In the same way that "nature vs. nurture" has been the wrong way to look at it for a while, "is it biology/society/etc" is the wrong way to look at the origins of mental disorder.
